CS10-17.note: With the explicit mention of distance removed, C now rests on inference from the mechanism: 'storms crossing a mountain front drop their heaviest water first, so the rain reaching the country beyond arrives already stripped' plus 'the fossils date the rise of the ranges upwind' - i.e. the ratio records what the air lost on its way past the barrier, which is path travelled, not local elevation. That inference is supported and unique. On the flagged risk: A is TEMPTING, NOT DEFENSIBLE. It is tempting because the amount effect is a real isotope effect and because 'drop their heaviest water first' is literally an amount statement, so a solver with genuine isotope knowledge will feel the pull. It fails on location and on the argument's shape: A places the signal in the basin's own seasons ('how much rain fell in the seasons when the leaves grew'), whereas Text 2's entire claim is that the basin's local conditions are irrelevant - 'whatever the ground beneath it is doing' - and that the signal was set upwind before the air arrived. Choosing A would have Text 2 substitute one local proxy for another, which is the opposite of its move. B (temperature) and D (post-burial exposure/evaporation) are likewise real isotope effects and therefore strong distractors; neither is raised by Text 2. The fact that all four options name genuine effects is what protects this item from the knowledge channel: subject knowledge alone cannot choose among them, only Text 2's mountain-front mechanism can.
